planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into sandy, slightly acidic soil at a pond or ditch margin; tolerates occasional flooding but resents drought and salt spray.

directions: A compact, non-aggressive wetland-edge shrub with bright yellow pollinator-magnet flowers all summer, this St. John's wort is useful for rain gardens, pond margins, and wet flatwoods restoration in the Deep South. Site it in sandy, slightly acidic soil that stays damp, keeping it out of coastal-exposed beds since it tolerates neither drought nor salt spray. Light, infrequent pruning after bloom keeps the needle-like foliage dense rather than leggy.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into damp, sandy, mesic-flatwoods-type soil; tolerates brief periods of standing water.

directions: Carrying near-year-round bloom peaking spring through fall, this small, tidy evergreen subshrub has distinctive heart-shaped clasping leaves and suits Gulf Coast rain gardens and pond-edge plantings where it tolerates brief inundation. Its Florida and Georgia-only native range makes it a strong regional-identity pick for Gulf Coast plantings specifically. Its clasping leaf bases and four-petaled flowers read as a genuinely different garden plant rather than another yellow Hypericum lookalike.

common_name: Early St. John's Wort (Naked-Flowered St. John's Wort)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall, or root summer softwood cuttings, into moist, humus-rich bottomland soil under high deciduous canopy.

directions: One of the very few Hypericum species that genuinely thrives in forest-interior shade, this deciduous understory shrub is a strong, differentiated pick for the shade-garden priority, useful along shaded streambanks and bottomland woodland edges. Its range just reaches the Florida Panhandle and eastern Texas, making it a legitimate though marginal Gulf Coast woodland option. Use it as a companion shrub layer beneath hardwoods along a shaded creek bank where summer yellow bloom is wanted but full sun isn't available.

planting.note: Direct-sow with 8 weeks cold-moist stratification into moist, well-drained soil in a part-shade border or woodland-edge planting; give it room to spread modestly by rhizome.

directions: A robust, showy herbaceous perennial rather than a dwarf shrublet like most of its relatives, this species carries large yellow flowers in midsummer, giving good vertical structure for a part-shade native border or rain garden. It tolerates rocky or slope sites better than most Hypericum and is more cold-hardy and northern in range than the Gulf Coast species in this collection, so it is best framed as a shade-tolerant native perennial option for northern or upland zones. Because it spreads by rhizome into small colonies, give it room rather than treating it as a tight specimen shrub.

common_name: Spotted St. John's Wort (Dotted St. John's Wort)

planting.note: Fall-sow directly outdoors and let winter cold do the stratification work, into average to dry-ish soil at a woodland margin or prairie edge.

directions: A clump-forming native perennial for woodland edges and part-shade meadows, easily told apart from the invasive common St. John's wort by the dark glandular dots covering its leaves and petals — a good native alternative, and its range reaches central peninsular Florida and eastern Texas, giving it genuine Gulf Coast relevance. It is more drought-tolerant than the Gulf Coast wetland species in this collection, making it useful for a part-shade bed that isn't consistently irrigated.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Sow with cold-moist stratification into open, low-competition, consistently wet acidic ground at the front of a bog garden.

directions: A diminutive, clump-forming wetland herb suited to bog gardens, pond margins, and wet pine-savanna restorations, this species fills a small-stature niche none of the existing shrubby Hypericum entries cover. It reaches southward to the Florida Panhandle and Mississippi, giving it legitimate, if modest, Gulf Coast relevance for wet pine savanna-style plantings. It won't compete with taller wetland natives, so give it open ground where it can colonize without crowding.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

common_name: Dwarf St. John's Wort (Common St. John's Wort)

planting.note: Surface-sow stratified seed without burying it into the base of a rain garden, pond shallow, or perpetually damp ditch line.

directions: A delicate, fine-textured small perennial or annual for consistently wet rain-garden bottoms or pond shallows where almost nothing else blooms yellow all summer, this species' wide native range from Newfoundland to south Florida and central Texas includes genuine Gulf Coast territory. It tolerates both the Gulf Coast's heat and much colder northern winters, an unusually broad-range species. It will self-sow modestly in consistently damp spots.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

common_name: Coppery St. John's Wort (Strict St. John's Wort)

planting.note: Plant into sandy or peaty acidic soil that stays consistently damp, in open to lightly shaded wet pine savanna conditions.

directions: A slender wet-pine-savanna perennial herb from the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, including a southern Alabama population, this species gives direct Gulf Coast relevance as one of the few Hypericum species in this collection with a true Gulf Coast disjunct population rather than just a Florida or Texas range tail. It is useful for wetland restoration plantings and as a lesser-known companion to the shrubby Hypericum species already in cultivation. Match its native wet pine savanna conditions as closely as possible with sandy or peaty acidic soil that stays consistently damp.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
